new_clusters.title: Music through the fly connectome, and a retraction
new_clusters.commentary: Audio pushed through the Janelia male CNS connectome as a leaky integrate-and-fire network, entering at 86 Johnston's organ afferents and leaving as MIDI from 56 descending neurons, with a companion video showing every neuron firing at its real anatomical position. Petkov then retracted half of his own headline result: the claim that signal is at chance two synapses in came from a single run, and across ten seeds the second-hop layer carries roughly 1-2% of the first hop's signal, detectable over ten runs but invisible in any one of them. The correction, not the music, is the most methodologically useful thing in this index.

items.title: Twenty seconds of music pushed through a fruit fly's connectome
items.author: Radoslav Petkov
items.text: The Janelia male CNS connectome, 165,122 neurons, 15 million synapses, simulated as a leaky integrate-and-fire network. Audio enters through 86 Johnston's organ afferents. Descending neuron firing rates come out as MIDI.

items.title: You can now watch it happen
items.author: Radoslav Petkov
items.text: Every dot in this video is a real neuron at its real position in the imaged animal, from Janelia's male Drosophila CNS volume: 165,122 traced neurons and roughly 15 million synaptic connections.

items.title: Half of it was wrong
items.author: Radoslav Petkov
items.text: The claim was that sound reaches the descending neurons across a single synapse, and that two synapses in the signal is at chance. That measurement ran once. Across ten seeds the two-synapse layer cleared significance in half the runs and missed in the other half.

The team says they deliberately used no external pretrained network so the fly 'can't cheat'; as with the knee-MRI build already indexed here, the comparison that would settle what the connectome contributes - a random graph of matched degree - is not reported.

items.title: Can a fly read X-rays? Actually, yes.

items.text: We built RadFly, a small research experiment using the fruit fly connectome as the basis of a neural network for medical image classification and trained the brain on a small subset of MIMIC-CXR. RadFly achieves an AUROC of over 80% on pleural effusion classification.

new_clusters.title: 165,122 neurons running on your own GPU, in the browser
new_clusters.commentary: A browser viewer that runs the male CNS wiring - 165,122 neurons by the author's count - in compute shaders on the visitor's own GPU, mapped onto a 3D fly, so escape, flight, grooming and feeding can each be traced to the neurons and muscles driving them. Built on the male CNS connectome, FlyWire, the Shiu et al. brain model and flybody, and credited as such; the post's 'nobody programmed those reactions' line understates the neuron-to-muscle mapping, which is engineering.

items.title: Fruit Fly: a real fruit fly's wiring map, running in your browser
items.author: Elbert P.
items.text: Fruit Fly is a real fruit fly's brain wiring with 165,122 neurons that is simulated with compute shaders and mapped to a 3D fly, so you can watch its neurons drive what it does. This site runs that map live on your own GPU in the local browser.

new_clusters.title: What the male connectome is, and what the game ports are not
new_clusters.commentary: An explainer on the MaleCNS release - 166,700 neurons and roughly 125 million synaptic connections, brain plus ventral nerve cord - and the Doom, Mario 64 and Beat Saber ports that followed within days. One of the few widely-shared posts to state plainly that a connectome is a wiring diagram rather than an upload, and that the Doom project's own documentation does not claim the fly learned to survive better over time.

items.title: Scientists mapped the male fruit fly CNS, then engineers connected it to Doom
items.author: Anna Simonova
items.author_title: Data Scientist | NLP Engineer | AI Engineer
items.text: It is important to be precise, though: this is a wiring diagram, not a literal upload of a fly's mind. A connectome tells us which neurons are connected, but it does not capture every electrical, chemical, and physiological detail of a living brain.

new_clusters.title: Virtual Fly Brain: where the data actually lives
new_clusters.commentary: A tour of Virtual Fly Brain as an access layer over the fly datasets - one anatomy ontology across every dataset and life stage, reachable from the browser, Python and R, an MCP endpoint and a chat interface. Infrastructure rather than a result, and the most direct answer in this index to where the connectome data comes from and how to query it.

items.title: Virtual Fly Brain: every fly connectome, image and gene in one place
items.author: Virtual Fly Brain

new_clusters.title: Every neuron in the male fly CNS, rendered
new_clusters.commentary: A nine-second 3D rendering of all neurons in the male fly brain and ventral nerve cord, published by the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology alongside the connectome and credited to Philipp Schlegel, with data from the Janelia FlyEM team, the Cambridge Connectomics Group, the MRC-LMB and Google Research. A visualization of the dataset, not a simulation running on it.

items.title: All neurons in the male fruit fly CNS
items.author: MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology

new_clusters.title: The optic lobe connectome, visualized
new_clusters.commentary: Janelia's visualization of the fruit fly optic lobe connectome, which they describe as mapping more than 50,000 neurons across more than 700 distinct types, showing the neuropils and some of the columnar neurons of the visual system. Predates the male CNS release by two years and is the sort of lab visualization the 2026 viral builds are layered on top of.

items.title: Columnar neurons from the Drosophila optic lobe
items.author: HHMI's Janelia Research Campus

new_clusters.title: FlyWire's own overview of the female whole-brain wiring diagram
new_clusters.commentary: FlyWire's summary of the female whole-brain connectome, stating 127,000 neurons, 32 million synapses, four years of work and 2.7 million manual edits, with renders by the project itself. Useful as the baseline figure set that the 2026 posts are usually misquoting or conflating with the male CNS numbers.

items.title: FlyWire Overview and Data Types

new_clusters.title: Querying the connectome, concretely
new_clusters.commentary: A short demo of FlyWire's connectivity app: picking a cell, pulling its upstream and downstream partners, and visualizing primary neurotransmitters and key neuropils. The tooling that makes 'query the connectome' a specific operation rather than a slogan.

items.title: FlyWire Connectivity App Demo
items.author: FlyWire Princeton

new_clusters.title: The first auditory connectome, and wiring that predicted responses
new_clusters.commentary: A visualization accompanying Baker et al. in Current Biology (2022), described as the first auditory connectome in any system: synaptic connectivity among more than 500 neurons across both hemispheres, 24 newly identified cell types, and a non-hierarchical network rather than separate pathways per sound. FlyWire's summary states the wiring diagram was able to predict auditory responses, which makes this a concrete precedent for the claim the viral builds gesture at.

items.title: Drosophila Auditory Connectome
items.author: FlyWire Princeton

new_clusters.title: Hacking the Fly Connectome: a hands-on workshop
new_clusters.commentary: A 2021 Virtual Fly Brain workshop on querying and analysing fly connectomics across neuPrint, CATMAID and VFB, with interactive Python and R notebooks and exercises on finding neurons by type, location, connectivity and morphological similarity. Five years old and still the most practical item in this index for working with the data rather than watching it.

items.title: Virtual Fly Brain: Hacking the Fly Connectome Workshop 2021
items.author: Virtual Fly Brain

new_clusters.title: Flappy Bird flapped by the giant fiber escape neuron
new_clusters.commentary: A game port that actually names its mechanism: a 'danger approaching' signal is injected into the visual looming neurons, propagated through the male CNS wiring to DNp01 (the giant fiber that runs from brain to the jump and flight muscles), and the bird flaps when DNp01 fires. The author states nothing is trained and that 166,700 neurons are simulated per game frame. Naming the output neuron rather than just claiming 'the fly plays X' is what separates this from most of the game ports.

items.title: Can a Fruit Fly Brain Play Flappy Bird?
items.author: NoloWiz
Rupesh Sreeraman
items.text: I used male fruit fly brain mapping to play Flappy Bird. When the bird is about to fall, I send a 'danger approaching' signal into the fly's looming neurons ... to the giant fiber (DNp01). If the giant fiber fires, the bird flaps. This is not AI. Nothing is trained.

new_clusters.title: A whole fly brain on a 15-pound touchscreen
new_clusters.commentary: The published FlyWire whole-brain model (Shiu et al., Nature 2024) run on a GBP 15 ESP32 display with 520 KB of RAM: the author states 138,639 neurons and 15 million connections, with only the few thousand neurons actually firing held in memory, the wiring of the ~2,100 that ever fire in flash, and the remainder on an SD card. He says every run checked on the board matches a reference simulation's spikes. The achievement is memory engineering, not new biology.

new_clusters.commentary: A real rover driven by a MaleCNS simulation: a hand rushed at the camera makes the escape circuit fire and the rover backs off and turns away, and a green ball makes it drive over. Unusually for this wave the description cites its sources - MaleCNS v1.0 from Janelia FlyEM (Berg et al., Cell 2026) for the wiring and Shiu et al. for the neuron model - so the claim is checkable rather than asserted.

The studio states plainly that the fly does not aim or fire - the game handles weapons automatically - and that enemy drones are translated into visual threat stimuli, so what is on display is escape circuitry reacting to synthetic looming input rather than a fly playing a game.

The same post reports that the identical circuit loses badly at Pong to a one-line if-statement. That negative result is the useful part: it is the clearest demonstration in this index that the connectome does the behaviour it evolved for and not the ones the game ports ask of it.

new_clusters.title: Connectome-constrained vision benchmarked against CNNs
new_clusters.commentary: A NeurIPS 2026 spotlight paper, announced by one of its authors, benchmarking FlyNet - a connectome-constrained model of the Drosophila visual system - against CNNs, RAFT and an unconstrained recurrent network on a looming collision-detection task. The authors report it matches or beats those architectures on common perturbations at up to five orders of magnitude fewer FLOPs, while giving up some of the adversarial robustness the unconstrained network keeps. This is the connectome used as a modelling constraint rather than as a demo.

new_clusters.title: A MaleCNS connectome playing Pokemon Emerald, live for three hours
new_clusters.commentary: A 2h48m live stream in which the MaleCNS v1.0 connectome, which the author gives as 166,700 neurons, is wired into Pokemon Emerald: the game screen is sampled through the model's photoreceptors and the buttons are pressed from its descending neurons. The author states the neurons are leaky integrate-and-fire units with constants from Shiu et al. (Nature, 2024), that the mushroom body is the only part that learns, and that no scripts or language model are involved. The on-screen panels show spiking activity, the dopamine signal and progress rungs, which is a readout of the simulation rather than evidence the fly understands the game.

items.title: Fruit fly connectome plays Pokemon Emerald | 166,700 simulated neurons, live

items.text: 166,700 neurons wired the way a real fly's are, getting the game screen through the fly's own photoreceptors and pressing buttons through its descending neurons. Wiring is MaleCNS v1.0 from Janelia/FlyEM; each neuron is a leaky integrate-and-fire unit with constants from Shiu et al. 2024. No scripts and no language model.

new_clusters.title: FlyCorp: four fly brains competing for three desks in MuJoCo
new_clusters.commentary: Episode seven of an ongoing series in which four copies of the FlyWire connectome, which the author gives as 138,639 simulated neurons each, drive office chairs in MuJoCo through the neurons that normally make a fly walk - P9 forward, MDN back, DNa02 for steering. The author says nothing is scripted and reports the trained brain reaching a desk roughly five times faster after thirty rounds of reward shaping, filmed at rounds 0, 15 and 30. The live panel plots every neuron at its mapped position as it spikes, so what is visible is connectome-derived activity steering a chair.

items.title: FlyCorp #7 The Reorg. 4 Fly Brains. 3 Desks. The Untrained Intern Kept His Job.
items.author: ipc0nfg
items.text: Four fruit fly brains (the FlyWire connectome, 138,639 simulated neurons each) drive office chairs in MuJoCo, seeing the office through their own simulated eyes. Desk school: 30 rounds, rewarded every 10 ms for getting closer to a desk. The exam: the trained brain got 5x faster to a desk.

new_clusters.title: A fly brain playing Gorilla Tag in VR
new_clusters.commentary: A VR channel's stunt video, 735,000 views in its first week, which says it taught a fly's open-source brain to move as a gorilla and play Gorilla Tag's infection mode across eight phases before the creator joins it in VR. Neither the video description nor the title names a dataset, a method or any code, so there is nothing to check the fly-brain claim against beyond the footage. It is both the highest-reach new item this run and the least documented one.

items.text: Using its open source brain, the fly learned to move around as a gorilla and got super good at it. It even learned how to play infection. In the end I actually play with it in VR.

new_clusters.title: Grey Leno: a talk show host puppeteered by a fly connectome
new_clusters.commentary: A browser-based late-night talk show whose host is driven by the FlyWire connectome, which the author gives as 138,639 neurons and 15.1M connections running from a 31MB file updated every 0.1ms. Unlike this account's earlier unsourced posts, the project ships as a public repo (github.com/SpikeCalls/grey-leno-fly-brain, JavaScript, created 2026-09-30) plus a live demo, so the claim that nobody writes the jokes or animates the body is at least inspectable. What it demonstrates is connectome-derived spiking driving a puppet rig, not comedy.

items.author: @SpikeCalls
items.text: SOMEONE JUST OPEN SOURCED GREY LENO, A TALK SHOW HOST CONTROLLED BY A REAL FRUIT FLY BRAIN WITH 138,639 NEURONS AND 0 WRITERS. That whole brain runs live in a browser tab from a 31 MB file, with every neuron updated every 0.1 ms.

items.text: GREY LENO IS A TALK SHOW HOST RUNNING ON A REAL UPLOADED FLY BRAIN WITH 138,639 NEURONS, 31 MB AND 0 WRITERS. Nobody wrote his jokes and nobody animated his body.

new_clusters.title: Shape sorter and colour sorting on a desktop fly brain
new_clusters.commentary: Two further episodes of the ongoing series on what the creator describes as a 139,255-neuron scanned fly brain running a body on his desk: a toddler's shape-sorter toy solved in 49 seconds, and ten balls sorted into same-coloured baskets, both rewarded with a cigarette box opening. His narration attributes deliberation to the fly - standing between the baskets rubbing its front legs, rolling a pyramid over after the square hole stops paying off - and the posts show neither the learning rule nor the simulator, so the behaviour is his account of it. The second post also notes that fruit flies are close to red-blind, which makes the red-versus-blue sorting the load-bearing claim of that episode.

items.author: @adamgrag
items.text: It just solved a toy made for toddlers in 49 seconds. A real scanned fruit fly brain, 139,255 neurons, running a body on my desk. Three shapes, three holes in a wall, and a shape through the right hole opens the cigarette box for 7 seconds.

items.author: @adamgrag
items.text: A fly that can barely see red just sorted red balls from blue ones. Fruit flies are close to red-blind. adamant, a scanned copy of a fruit fly brain with 139,255 neurons, got 10 balls in two colours today. The cigarette door opens only when every ball sits in the basket of the same colour.

new_clusters.title: One fly brain to mimic one rat neuron
new_clusters.commentary: A one-line claim with video from a computational neuroscientist: that one fly brain can almost perfectly mimic one rat neuron, which would put a whole fly connectome at roughly the compute needed to reproduce a single cortical neuron's input-output function. The post cites no paper, method or figures and has no thread behind it, so the comparison rests on the author's say-so; it is included because the claim is specific and comes from someone working in the field.

items.author: @IdoAizenbud
items.text: One fly brain can almost perfectly mimic one rat neuron.

new_clusters.title: A world for the fly, with the connectome not yet plugged in
new_clusters.commentary: The fourth instalment of a FlyWire-based project built in public: a 3D room with drifting obstacles and glowing food in which a fly navigates autonomously. The author states plainly that the navigation is hand-coded ray-casting and angle-seeking rather than the spiking circuit from his earlier phases, and calls the environment a labelled placeholder built so the connectome-derived circuit has somewhere to be plugged in next. Worth indexing as the rare entry in this wave whose author says up front that the connectome is not driving what you are watching.

items.title: A visual milestone: the fly finally has a world to live in
items.author: Raunak Sharma
items.text: Built a small 3D environment: a walled room, scattered obstacles, glowing food. Important honesty check: the fly's brain right now is simple hand-coded steering logic - ray-casting for obstacle avoidance, angle-seeking toward the nearest food. It is NOT yet driven by the actual spiking neural circuit from Phases 0-3.

new_clusters.title: The fly connectome as a latency problem, and then as an ASIC
new_clusters.commentary: An ASIC and FPGA engineer works out what it would cost to run the fly connectome at its real timing, reporting that even a coarse feed-forward approximation binning about 160,000 neurons into 122 bins comes to roughly 600M multiply-accumulates per step, and that the connectome's 2ms ingress-to-egress path with 0.1ms internal updates is beyond any GPU he can find or imagine. His follow-up moves the connectome logic to silicon instead, showing a SkyWater 130nm ASIC layout with a rough 50mW power estimate. Every figure is his own estimate from his own synthesis work; no benchmark, measurement or tapeout is shown.

items.title: Replicating the fly connectome with a feed-forward model, and why a GPU cannot keep up
items.author: Damir Wallener
items.text: I can roughly replicate the Fly connectome with a feed-forward LLM. 250k ish parameters, but 600M ish MACs is a problem when the fly is running at 0.1ms integration time, and the granularity is coarse: 160k neurons in 122 bins. The fly connectome has a 2ms cycle path. If we drop the AI model and build a chip to match the connectome, rough estimate is we can do it on 50mW.

items.title: Fly connectome logic as an ASIC in SkyWater 130nm
items.author: Damir Wallener
items.text: Fly connectome logic as an ASIC in SkyWater 130nm. Posted as layout images with no accompanying text.

new_clusters.title: A fly connectome ranking apartment listings
new_clusters.commentary: A FlyWire connectome, which the author gives as about 140,000 neurons and 54.5 million synapses, used to rank apartment listings in Limassol: hard filters run in ordinary code, then each listing photo is compressed to an 8x8 grid of 192 numbers and pushed through the connectome, with would-visit / maybe / not-for-me feedback shaping the ranking after a few examples. He states that the neuron positions, cell types and wiring come from published connectome data but the dynamics, input encoding and scoring are his own, and that the result proves nothing about how flies think. The demo shows activity propagating through real connectome neurons when a listing photo is clicked.

items.title: I hired a fly to find me an apartment in Limassol
items.author: Andrei Domashkevich
items.author_title: Product Manager | AI agents, LLM applications & automation
items.text: Each apartment photo is compressed into an 8x8 grid, 192 numbers in total, and pushed through the connectome. I give it feedback: would visit, maybe, not for me. A necessary disclaimer: I am not simulating an actual fly. The dynamics, input encoding and the way neural activity becomes an apartment score are mine. This proves absolutely nothing about how flies think.

new_clusters.title: The connectome as an excavated city, not a mind
new_clusters.commentary: A short critique arguing that a wiring diagram is not a mind: the author likens the connectome to a perfectly excavated ancient city whose streets, intersections and foundations are all visible but whose traffic rules, economics and culture are not, and says dropping activity into static architecture does not bring the city to life. It is a counterpoint to the game ports and mind-uploading claims rather than a build of its own.

The author states the fly layer gets 25% of the final score, that a giant-fiber escape reflex can hard-block an action once learned valence drops below a set threshold, and that the reference graph is MaleCNS at 166,606 neurons and 25.5M edges. He is explicit that there are no spiking neurons and no claim to simulate a real fly, calling the system connectome-constrained rather than connectome-faithful.

items.title: The effect of fruit fly's brain neurons on LLM agent behaviour
items.author: Oppa AI
items.text: Currently doing research and test on the fly-brain neurons connectome as a biological simulation layer inside the brain of my local AI companion running on a Jetson Orin Nano. Modulatory only. The LLM proposes, the fly votes. The fly gets 25% of the final score. One veto: a giant fiber escape reflex can hard-block an external action, and only when learned valence drops below -0.6. Deliberately NOT included: spiking neurons, automatic weight tuning, or any claim of simulating a real fly. It's connectome-constrained, not connectome-faithful. The reference graph is MaleCNS (166,606 neurons, 25.5M edges).

new_clusters.title: A digital fly that looked like it followed light, and did not
new_clusters.commentary: A two-part build log: Mykola Bondarenko wires a simulated fruit-fly brain into a WebGL body with the goal of having a drone explore an unknown building, then reports that his own phototaxis result was an artifact — he states that almost every visual stimulus eventually produced the same saturated escape response. The follow-up describes building a headless twin of the environment and evolving the modelling parameters while leaving the connectome itself untouched. The creator debunking his own earlier clip is rarer than anything else in this index.

items.author: Mykola Bondarenko
items.text: What if a drone could explore an unknown building using a simulated fruit-fly brain instead of a traditional AI model? That is the experiment I'm building. [video: Can a Digital Fly Brain Explore ...]

items.author: Mykola Bondarenko
items.text: In my first experiment, I connected a digital fruit-fly brain to a virtual body and watched it climb toward the light. It looked surprisingly natural, and I assumed I was seeing phototaxis. I was wrong. When I started testing the brain directly, I discovered that almost every visual stimulus eventually produced essentially the same saturated escape response. That discovery changed the whole project. I built a headless twin of the WebGL environment, started evolving the modeling parameters without changing the connectome itself, and tried to answer a harder question: Can this fly actually explore an unknown room?

new_clusters.title: Asking a connectome which stripes a fly notices
new_clusters.commentary: Varun Reddy reports running 617 fabric patterns and 240 trap designs through an open-source model of the fly visual system, says it reproduced three results from live-fly experiments it was never given, and flags an apparently untested question: how wide the stripes on a fly trap should be. The post names neither the model nor the three results, so the reproduction claim is his and is not checked here; the appeal is that it asks the connectome a question with an answer outside it.

items.author: Varun Reddy
items.text: A fruit fly's visual system has been mapped synapse by synapse, and the model built on it is open source. I ran 617 fabric patterns and 240 trap designs through it. It reproduced three results from live-fly experiments it was never given — and pointed at a gap: nobody appears to have tested how wide the stripes on a fly trap should be.
